newsitem.title: UK: UK's Clarke doesn't see UK joining new ERM grid.
newsitem.headline: UK's Clarke doesn't see UK joining new ERM grid.

text.p: British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said on Sunday he did not think it would be in Britain's interest to join a new version of the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM), dubbed ERM II. "I just don't think that's suitable for the United Kingdom. I don't contemplate going into a second ERM if we stay outside," said Clarke, speaking on BBC radio.

European finance ministers met this weekend in Dublin and agreed on a broad structure for "ERM II", which would be designed for countries waiting to join a single European currency after its initial launch, planned for 1999.
Britain withdrew sterling from the original ERM in September 1992 after intense speculation in foreign exchange markets pushed it lower.
But Clarke also said it would be the "worst policy" for Britain to dither and then join a European monetary union late.
"That would be the worst policy of all with the British doing their traditional business of not being able to make their minds up and then joining late. That I think would be pathetic," he said.
The informal talks in Dublin, which included central bank governors, laid the foundations for three critical areas of monetary union, taking a giant leap towards the realisation of a single currency.

As well as the architecture for ERM II, which would limit fluctuations between a newly-launched euro and currencies waiting to join when their economies are ready, EU ministers reached agreement on a so-called stability pact and on greater legal assurances over EMU for banks and businesses.
The stability pact is designed to set penalties for countries that fail to maintain strict fiscal stances after EMU.

Britain's Conservative government has retained the right to opt out of any single currency and the party wrangles internally between pro-Europeans such as Clarke and right-wing "Eurosceptics" who want the government to reject EMU. Last week, foreign secretary Malcolm Rifkind bolstered Eurosceptic confidence with a keynote speech warning that EMU could tear Europe apart. But Clarke on Sunday said Britain should make its choice on whether to join in EMU "at the most sensible moment," which he suggested was around a year before EMU went ahead.

"At the most sensible moment, which is the last possible moment to exercise our option, the British should take advantage of the fact that we have a choice as to whether we should join or not," he said.
He added whether Britain should join or not "can only be decided about 12 months before the players are going ahead."
